introduction: These readings ask for attention. Scattered thought achieves nothing and concentrated thought much; whoever undertakes a thing should give the whole self to it; prayer needs a mind not wandering to the body or the window; and beyond tasks and prayers there is a continuous remembrance of God, in standing and sitting, at the plough and at rest, whose opposite the readings call heedlessness, 'the worst calamity'. All twenty-three quotations are read here beside twenty-three from elsewhere. Most stand alongside: 'one thing is needful', Paul's 'this one thing I do', the Preacher's 'do it with thy might', Deuteronomy's words kept when sitting, walking and rising, Herbert's swept room, the Dhammapada on earnestness, Claudius finding that 'words without thoughts never to heaven go'. Two add a side: Zhuangzi's mind as a mirror that holds nothing, and Confucius remarking of a man who always thought three times that twice would do.
questions: 'So long as the thoughts of an individual are scattered he will achieve no results.' Where is your attention most divided, and what would gathering it take?
What do the readings ask of the mind in prayer, and how does Hamlet's king show the lack of it?
Remembrance is asked 'in thy standing and thy sitting'. How can a mind be on its work and on God at once? What does Herbert suggest?
Zhuangzi's perfect man holds nothing in his mind. Is that the opposite of concentration, or another name for it?
Thoughtlessness is called the worst calamity. What public events would you explain that way?

outside.why: Jesus told Martha that she was careful and troubled about many things, but one thing is needful.
Paul says: this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, I press toward the mark.
Ecclesiastes says: whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might.
Paul tells the Colossians: whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men.
A psalm says: O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee.
Paul lists what the mind should dwell on, the true, the just, the pure, the lovely, and says: think on these things.
A king at prayer in Hamlet admits: my words fly up, my thoughts remain below; words without thoughts never to heaven go.
Jesus advised: when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and shut thy door.
Isaiah says: thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee.
Paul's rule for the Thessalonians was to rejoice evermore, pray without ceasing, and in every thing give thanks.
The Qur'an says that it is in the remembrance of God that hearts find rest.
Deuteronomy asks that the words be spoken of when thou sittest in thine house, and walkest by the way, and liest down, and risest up.
George Herbert prays to see God in all things, and says that who sweeps a room as for his laws makes the action fine.
Paul asks: know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you?
The first psalm blesses the one whose delight is in the law of the Lord, and who meditates in it day and night.
The Dhammapada says that earnestness is the path of immortality, and thoughtlessness the path of death.
Zhuangzi says the perfect man uses his mind as a mirror: it responds to what comes, and does not retain it. Is mindfulness holding a thought fast, or holding nothing?
Tennyson says: speak to him, for he hears; closer is he than breathing, and nearer than hands and feet.
When Confucius heard of a man who always thought thrice before acting, he said: twice may do. Can care about consequences become its own fault?
Confucius said that learning without thought is labour lost, and thought without learning is perilous.
Paul wrote that now it is high time to awake out of sleep.
The Dhammapada praises the one who is earnest among the thoughtless, awake among the sleepers.
Mark says that Jesus rose a great while before day, went out into a solitary place, and there prayed.
